strengths: Originality: The joint treatment of image resolution, deformation complexity, and sample size provides an interesting statistical perspective. The strongest contribution is the proposed quantitative understanding of classification under geometric variability.

Significance: The framework offers a useful theoretical benchmark for distinguishing finite-resolution ambiguity from insufficient training data. The alignment approach in Section 3.2 is particularly concrete and potentially useful in settings with controlled backgrounds and deformations.

Technical merits: Support rescaling and brightness normalization provide an explicit mechanism for approximately invariant representations. The CNN construction using deformed template filters and global max-pooling also gives an interpretable representational argument.

Presentation: The progression from the observation model through classifiers, theory, and experiments is easy to follow. Figures 2, 4, and 6 clarify the constructions, and the extensive appendices make the arguments inspectable.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript appropriately acknowledges computational difficulties with exact 0–1 optimization, background noise, partial visibility, and the multiple-template experiment extending beyond the theory. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the mathematical analysis and MNIST-based experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation (27) does not define empirical misclassification minimization. It minimizes −(1/n)Σ k_i·1{q_2(X_i)>1/2}, which never penalizes false positives because k_i is in {0,1}. Consequently, the classifier that always predicts 1 is an empirical minimizer, with population error 1−π even for separable classes. The claimed equivalence in Equation (94) is therefore false, and the application of Lemma B.8 does not establish Theorem 4.1 for the defined estimator. The objective must be corrected and the resulting argument checked.

Soundness: The proof of Theorem 3.1 contains a consequential quantifier error. Lemma A.3 establishes closeness to the normalized template for a suitable approximate inverse B*, but page 29 applies this bound to every B_i and B in the classifier's minimization. An arbitrary inverse candidate need not undo the generating deformation. Moreover, Equation (12) does not control all compositions introduced by independently transforming both images. For example, with A={I,R_90} and an asymmetric template f_1=f_0 composed with R_180, the forward class orbits can be separated while inverse-transformed candidates from opposite classes coincide. Thus cross-class ties can persist at arbitrarily high resolution, contradicting the claimed strict separation of classifier distances.

Soundness of optimality: Theorem 3.7 constructs pixel-indistinguishable templates with ordinary L2 distance of order at least 1/d. However, the classification conditions use D, which minimizes over brightness and geometric transformations. A lower bound on ordinary L2 distance does not establish a lower bound on D. The construction needs an additional argument showing separation in the same metric before it establishes the advertised optimality of the separation rate.

Presentation and mathematical precision: Theorem 4.2, Lemma 4.3, and the statement of Proposition B.4 reference the separation quantity in Equation (21), whereas the general CNN proof uses Equation (12). These quantities are different: Equation (21) only optimizes axis-wise scaling and translation, while Equation (12) accommodates the general deformation class. Their interchange leaves the hypotheses unclear for rotations and nonlinear deformations.

Significance: The CNN learning guarantee, even after correcting the objective, concerns exact empirical minimization over a specially chosen architecture. Its complexity term scales as |A_d|²/n up to logarithms, with |A_d|≥d². This provides a specialized existence and sample-complexity result, but offers limited explanation of practical CNN training or performance with few examples.

Evaluation: Section 5 provides illustrative evidence for alignment on synthetic deformations, but does not test the central resolution-dependent claims: d remains 28, template separation is not varied, and general nonlinear deformations are not evaluated. The trained CNN architectures also differ from the analyzed construction. Medians from 30 repetitions with 100 test images, without variability estimates, provide limited support for fine performance comparisons.

Reproducibility: The experimental description omits deformation parameter ranges and distributions, training epochs, batch size, training loss, and precise template selection or seeds. Interpolation and boundary handling are also relevant to the observation model and full-visibility assumptions but are unspecified. No implementation or code link is provided. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of the CNN comparisons.
